purpose: Doxorubicin is a powerful chemotherapy medicine used to treat several types of cancer, including breast cancer, bladder cancer, leukemia, and lymphoma. It is often given along with other cancer medicines as part of a treatment plan. Your cancer care team chose this medicine because it can help slow down or stop cancer cell growth.
how_it_works: This medicine works by getting inside cancer cells and damaging their DNA, which is like the cell's instruction manual. When the DNA is damaged, the cancer cells cannot grow or copy themselves anymore and they eventually die. Because it targets fast-growing cells, it is very effective against cancer, though it can also affect some healthy fast-growing cells in your body.
common_side_effects: Nausea and vomiting, hair loss (usually temporary), mouth sores, loss of appetite, fatigue and weakness, low blood counts (which can increase infection risk and cause easy bruising or bleeding), and your urine may turn red or pink for a day or two after treatment — this is normal and not harmful.
warnings: This medicine can weaken your heart over time, so your doctor will monitor your heart health regularly. It can cause serious harm to your veins if it leaks out during the IV infusion, so tell your nurse right away if you feel any burning or pain at the injection site. It can lower your immune system, so avoid people who are sick and report any fever over 100.4°F (38°C) immediately. It is not safe during pregnancy and can affect fertility. Always tell your doctor about all other medicines you take.
typical_dosing: Doxorubicin is given through an IV (into a vein) by a nurse or doctor in a clinic or hospital — you will not take this as a pill at home. The dose and schedule depend on your specific cancer type, body size, and treatment plan. A common schedule is once every 3 weeks, but your oncology team will tell you exactly what to expect for your personal treatment plan.
